Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Red Eye.
I'm your host, Eddie Palmgen, and with me in the studio is my friend and colleague, Niklas Savos.
In today's episode, we are joined by J.C. the Swan.
The Swan is a lecturer in the economics department at Princeton University.
He teaches courses on ethics in finance and on Asian capital markets,
and is also a partner at Cornwall Capital, an investment fund based in New York City.
In the book and subsequent movie, The Big Short, author Michael Lewis wrote that
Cornwall Capital was one out of fewer than 20 investors in the world, who saw, in short,
the subprime mortgage market before its collapse.
So, Nicholas, which book will we speak about today?
The title for this episode is J.C. de Swan's book, Seeking Virtue in Finance,
where we will learn about the ethical aspects that finance professionals encounter.
And what do you think makes this book relevant for us and our listeners?
Seeking virtue in finance gives many examples of good and bad behavior, and from these
examples, I think there is a lot to learn for analysts, investors and operators.
The mission of the book is also aligned with our core values at Investing by the Books and Redi to show
that there are many good people in finance who strive to make a positive difference for the world.
I think the following quote sums up what the Swan aims to do with this book.
The fundamental question I seek to address is how, given the existing structures and set
of incentives in the finance industry, a finance professional can pursue a viable career
while benefiting society and upholding humanistic values.
Seeking virtue in finance was published in 2020 by Cambridge University Press, and we are delighted
delighted to have its author on the show today. Here comes our conversation with J.C. the Swan.
Hello, Jaycey, and welcome to Investing by the Books podcast.
Great. Thanks so much for having me today.
We're delighted to have you on and thank you for taking the time. So where are we reaching
you today? So I'm in my apartment in New York City. I live in New York and I commute to Princeton
on the days I teach. And to begin, can you tell our listeners about your background and how you got to where
you are today? Sure. So I divide my time between investing, teaching and writing. I've been
teaching at Princeton for the last 15 years or so, and I teach courses on Asian
economies in capital markets and on ethics and finance, and I also work closely with undergraduates as a faculty
advisor. On the investment side, I've been with Cornwall Capital for about a dozen years,
and I've been doing a combination of macro investing and in recent years, in recent years, shareholder activism in Japan as
well as some private activity. Now, in terms of my background, I started by studying both
geopolitics and history of art separately as an undergraduate. And then I did a combination of
geopolitics, economic development, and public policy, and grad school.
And after that, I ended up working at McKinsey in management consulting for a number of years and
eventually moved to the byside. But I came to the byside from a little bit of an unusual angle in the sense
that I'd always been interested in this concept of finances of force for good as a way to promote
economic development, and I wanted to, I was particularly interested in investing in
emerging markets. And so I started by being an analyst that in Asia dedicated long short equity fund and
then worked for a macro fund. And it's really in the last 15 years or so that I took a little bit of
a hybrid path that combined investing in teaching. And I have to say I've been
incredibly lucky to be able to do that. So far, it's worked in part because the two
activities are quite symbiotic. They reinforce each other. And also because I have partners who have been very supportive.
I'm curious if there was a specific moment in your life where, where you realize that this is what I want
to do? Well, certainly, so I guess there are two aspects. One of them is on the teaching side, I
So I grew up in Paris, I'm French and American, and I moved to the States to go to college.
And there I was mesmerized by some of the lectures and some of the professors and some of the professors,
and I thought, wow, I want to do that. And I started teaching in graduate school. And it
was by far the most challenging thing I'd ever done. And it forced me to delve so much deeper
into the topic and really in order to be able to be able to not only that presented,
but answer questions and discuss it and debated. And I thought it was incredibly enriching. And I wanted
to do that. But at the same time, I wasn't as excited about doing a pure academic research.
And so I also developed an interest over time in investing.
And I think there's a particular book that was interesting that really got me excited about investing,
which is a book about macro investing that I read when it was in my early 20s.
So that's the inception of these interest points.
And today we will speak about your book seeking virtue in finance.
Why did you choose to write it?
So I, you know, so I was always interested in this concept of finance as a force for good.
And when I started teaching, a natural course for me to create was one on ethics and finance and
on the impact of finance on society.
And I, so I taught this course to, so the ethics and finance specifically, I taught it to undergraduates.
And I found repeatedly that many of my students are keen to work in finance, but they're concerned about
being corrupted the minute they walk into their first job, right, whatever the first job is in finance,
whether it's investment banking or private equity or hedge fund.
And the other thing that was striking also is that the first semester I taught the course on ethics and finance, halfway through the first semester, one student asked me, why is it that our discussions put so much emphasis on unethical behavior?
Why don't we also analyze constructive behavior?
Why don't we talk about inspiring people?
And I thought, of course, why is it that we never
devoted any attention to this. So I looked for the literature to bolster the syllabus
and to devote attention to it, but I couldn't find any. So I decided to embark on this as a research project,
tied to my course, and out of it came the book Seeking Virtue and Finance.
And when we speak about virtue, that reminds me of Ryan Holliday's book series
on different virtues. But for those not familiar with it, how would you define
virtue? So the way I approach it, first of all, is influenced by Aristotelian
philosophy and virtue ethics. And virtue ethics tends to call for living in a way that's consistent with
virtues and calls for exercising practical wisdom in the face of challenges and dilemmas. Now, I didn't set out
to write the book with an explicit objective to apply virtue ethics to finance.
But I ended up drawing from its tradition and I would say drawing in particular from the fact that
virtue ethics emphasizes moral character, practical wisdom. It also emphasizes moderation.
And I think that is particularly useful in finance where we see a lot of excessive behavior.
And it also aspires to achieve both moral and skill-based excellence, which I found very compelling.
And there's a lot of emphasis on leading by example.
So now, going back to your question, I took all of this and I defined virtue simply as the ability to
to balance your self-interest with the collective interest with the collective interest despite the
pressure to conform to industry norms that, you know, often push us to focus on the
short-term profit maximizing path, right? And what I did in order to study virtue is I studied role models.
And I looked for individuals that were self-interested, ambitious, successful. I
I wasn't looking for people that were altruistic because it's hard to relate to altruistic because it's hard
to relate to altruism. So I looked for these people that were self-interested
and yet they were able to balance their self-interest and the collective interests. And from that,
I teased out a framework that defines virtue virtue more specifically along the ability to follow four
pillars of conduct, you know, over the course of a career.
And we will go deeper into those soon. But first, I would like to ask you
a bit about the difference between the popular culture today, which portrays finance
pretty poorly compared to you who write in the book that the premise of it is that finance is a force for
good. Why do you think this difference exists?
Yeah, so, so that's an interesting point because, so first of all, I should mention my
my fundamental belief is that finance is a force for good. So that's my starting point.
And what's interesting is that our understanding of finance as a force for good has evolved over the years.
When I was a grad student studying economic development, we never spoke about finance or banking
as a factor in economic development. And it's only in the 1990s that there's a new area of
research that developed, there was a guy in Northwestern, there was a guy at Brown,
another one at the World Bank. And they started identifying ways in which finance had positive spillover effects
effects on economies, on societies. And from that moment on, I think, at least in the academic world,
there was the sense that finance is more than simply the plumbing. And the
research showed that it tends to help economic growth, creates more opportunities for a broader
population, tends to spur entrepreneurship, promotes innovation, improves corporate governance,
all sorts of ways in which it's helpful.
So that was kind of a whole trend in the 1990s in the 2000s. But then the global financial crisis
came along, and that absolutely shattered these notions, right? And it brought to
for the fact that not all finance is a force for good, and that there can be such a thing
as too much finance.
And so that's, I think, I think, one, and there's also the rise of inequality, and these things combined to
spur often a negative impression of finance in popular culture.
And, but to me, it was really interesting that pivot in the research to the research to
the limitations of finance and ways in which certain types of finance can create
create their own problems. Now, you know, I'll, I'll just add to this, you know, again, my view is finance
is absolutely a force for good, but it does have limitations. And at times, it sways away from its
client-serving mission, and it sways away from its singular focus on supporting the real
economy.
And you mentioned the four pillars, which is also how you have
structured the book. Can you briefly introduce the listeners to it?
So these are the pillars that I teased out of the study of these role models. And, you know, very simply,
so four pillars, the first pillar is customer mandate. And this is the most important
pillar. It is our professional mandate, since we're in the business of serving customers.
And the key here is to serve your customer's interest,
faithfully, even when no one is looking. And that's the challenge, of course, that in finance,
there's a lot of opportunity to self-serve, to in a way, extract value from your customers, because it's
often the case that the relevant information for customers is hard to find or it's difficult to
interpret. And so you can think of that pillar as a spectrum, right? And on one hand,
you have putting your client's interests first,
and all the way to fleecing clients and proverbial grab what you can, when you can.
So that's the first pillar. And I think traditionally, when people thought about ethics and finance,
they thought about that fiduciary responsibility to their customers, rightly so, right?
And then the second pillar is social wealth creation. And this pillar, this pillar, in a sense,
is rooted in a conundrum.
because you could find yourself in situations where you serve your customers very well, and you fulfill your primary customer mandate, but you do so by extracting value from other stakeholders or from society. And so this pillar is really about serving your customers well without extracting value from others at a minimum, and ideally by creating value for other stakeholders.
The third pillar is inclusive leadership.
And here now we're looking inwardly inside the organization.
So whatever firm you work at.
And in my mind, I was started curious that when we talked about ethics, we didn't really talk about
the way in which you interacted with colleagues, with employees.
And to me, it's very hard to think of someone as virtuous if they're
being horrible to their colleagues and employees. And so the questions asked in the third
pillar is, are you treating your colleagues and employees with dignity and humanity? Are you helping
them develop and thrive? And are you preventing discrimination? So these are all relevant questions
in my mind. Now, in the hierarchy of these four pillars, I don't think it's as important as the first two
because we're talking about a smaller community now, like, it's a small group of, you know,
employees and colleagues, but it matters in my mind.
And finally, the fourth pillar engaged citizenship.
And that, you know, to me, that was the one that was the one that was most fun, most interesting to
research, because the premise here is that as finance professionals were lucky in that we
have a skill set that's very versatile.
And this pillar is really.
really about to what extent are you using your skill set and perhaps the network that
you've developed in the industry and potentially, if you've had a lot of success, any wealth you might have
generated, to serve society outside of the parameters of your job in finance.
And it can be in parallel to it, or it can be, you know, once you've moved on from the
industry. So at a very high level, these are the four pillars.
And if we start with how to serve customers well, you bring up the point that the goal
for the individual working in the finance industry typically is to make as much money as possible,
which is often at odds with the customers. Do you have a good example of that?
Yeah, I mean, I'll mention, you know, so first of all, finance professionals are naturally
incentivized to do well, right, by their customers. And, and they need to be competitive in order
to survive and create demand for their financial services.
But now, this being said, there's a lot of opportunity to extract value for your customers.
And that is because the industry is complex, it's opaque, and it's opaque often by design.
And there's a large asymmetry of information between the service provider and the service provider,
particularly on the retail side. So in terms of examples, there's a lot of interesting
examples in academic research, in fact, that shows that shows that some of the most complex retail products,
which tend to generate some of the highest profit margins, they also tend to be targeted at households
that are the least likely to understand them. Because they are the ones that are more likely to
sign up for them, right? And so they were egregious examples of structured retail products
that essentially were exotic options on equities being sold to customers at savings banks in places
like France. And savings banks, of course, tend to service lower income households.
And, and, you know, of course, these households are the least likely to understand
these products. And lo and behold, these products often often didn't perform well for
customers. So, so there are all sorts of examples like this. There are examples in the credit
card industry where the least attractive credit cards end up being targeted at the households
least likely to understand the terms and so on. But, you know, the the caveat here is, I think
most of finance serves its customers well. And so I don't want to leave the impression that
everybody's out there, the fleece clients, but there is a space where, you know, this happens
and it's reasonably frequent.
And a recurring theme of the book is otherwise that you describe individuals and companies that have set
good examples for the industry.
And in this chapter about serving the customers, well, you mentioned Jack Bogle,
which most of our listeners probably is familiar with, but
Why is he, in your view, a good example?
Yeah, so Jack Bogle is a towering figure.
As, as you know, he founded Vanguard, the pioneer low-cost index fund manager, and he has arguably
created more social value than just about anyone in finance, in the U.S., at least, over the past
decades. I was very lucky in that he was involved in my seminar for many years before
he passed away. And his life's mission was very simply to persuade individual savers to move from active
asset management to passive index funds. And it was based on a view that they would just be much better off
with these types of products. Even if it generated dramatically lower fees to him as
the financial service provider. And he had a strong belief that the asset management industry
was a gigantic exercise in collusion amongst the leading asset management firms to fleece the customers.
And so he started a revolution in the asset management industry towards index products and
more fees. And he truly worked on behalf of his customers' interests. And frankly,
he was not popular amongst his peers because.
is he put so much downward pressure on fees across the industry, right?
And the other thing that's remarkable about about him is, I mean, this is someone that, you know,
that had been very successful already in the fund management world.
He had to leave his previous company.
He could have started all sorts of ventures.
he decided to set up Vanguard as a not-for-profit.
It's a mutual company where all the profits are returned to customers in the form of lower fees, in the form of lower fees, which, you know, frankly, makes it hard for, you know, companies competing against Vanguard.
So he's absolutely remarkable.
And, you know, and one of things that's always been an interesting debate with him was, why is it that it
took 40 years for the revolution to happen because all of the data, all the empirical
research, you know, came out in the early 1970s. And it's really in the last, what, 15 years that we saw the dramatic
ramp up. So that that was always a source of interesting, you know, debate with him and discussion in the
classroom. Was there something else you took away from all the speaks and talks that he had
at Princeton every year? Yeah, I mean, you know, you know, it's interesting because
So I'm always keen to meet role models.
And he's one of the role models that I probably admire more after seeing him up close.
And, you know, frankly, that's not true of all the role models.
And your heroes, you know, the closer you get to them and the more you realize they're human.
And so sometimes it's better to see them from afar.
What I liked about him is that on one hand,
he was a driven evangelist who was really trying to convert people to the idea that
that low cross index fund should be the core of your savings for, you know, for most people.
And but at the same time, I love the fact that he, he was realistic and he was very open-minded in the sense
that he didn't put down at all people who worked in hedge funds or private equity.
And he saw them as creating value in their own way, and that he saw them as an important part of the financial system.
And, you know, and at the end of the day, his issue ultimately was about investment products that were misrepresented and over Christ.
You know, and the other thing I might add is that getting to interact with him up close,
one challenge about including him as one of the role models in the book is that
he was so not materialistic that it was, you know, it's almost hard to relate to him.
Like, people are not like that.
Like, there was something about him that he was just absolutely not interested in money.
And that, that's very unusual, right?
So I, you know, I thought that was, that was interesting as well.
And did you understand more deeply why he was drive, why was his personal goal to drive this
change in the industry and also to give back so much to,
to society in that sense?
Unclear, what, you know, he had a very, very strong Christian faith.
He'd also been brought up as a scholarship student and always wanted to give back.
And but ultimately, I think he was, you know, less interested in generating wealth for himself
than generating a reputation as someone who had a tremendous impact on society.
And as you, as you know,
As you mentioned, one of the problems that he tried to solve was, of course,
the excessive fees that many, many fund managers take for managing money.
And you bring up a few examples of funds that have structures that are quite interesting.
And one of them is the model of Orbis investments, which charges a 0.45% management fee
and a 25% fee on any profits generated above the MSCI World Index.
which is like the traditional hedge fund structure, I guess, many, many funds charges
a higher management fee.

How has their track record been and how has the AUM growth been?
And also I want to ask, why do you think so few managers have followed
of this type of structure.
Yeah, so that's a very good question.
Now, I, you know, I think, I think they're a very interesting fun, right? Because they do something
that very few funds do.
They basically, who try to create symmetry between them and their customers, right?
And there's something deeply asymmetric in the hedge fund industry.
about taking incentive fees every year when you make a profit and then not
not taking incentive fee when you make a loss, but of course, what happens is that your limited partners end
up leaving the fund if you underperform, but they don't reimburse you your fees.
And so you end up generating higher fees than really what's, you know, you know,
meant to be on paper at the end of the day.
And he and a few others that I've, or he, he, Orbus, and a few other funds that I've studied and a few other funds
that I've studied have done this, a very thoughtful, uh, very thoughtful, or adopted this very thoughtful
approach of creating symmetry.
And it's like they generate a profit, they take an incentive and they generate a loss and

So now,

And the last I saw was something like low teens compound annual return in, you know, and this is
